prompt.context: Our client is a private equity firm that is looking to invest in a gym chain. They are looking at two potential acquisitions and are trying to determine which one is more attractive. Each gym chain has 150 gyms across the U.S. in the same geographies. Assume no market growth; the market is fragmented. Both chains are premium gyms that price themselves the same. Assume the capital structure of the PE deal is the same for both, and that management at both gyms is skilled and happy to sell to PE.
prompt.question: Walk me through how the private equity firm should evaluate the gyms.

clarifying_info.q: What are the drivers of user/member growth?
clarifying_info.a: Seasonality (summer vs. winter) and annual contracts expiring. Two key metrics are churn rate and acquisition cost/rate — why people might sign up at different times of year.

clarifying_info.q: What does the cost structure look like?
clarifying_info.a: Fixed costs are a substantial portion of the business. Key fixed cost items include lease, maintenance, SG&A, and staff.

Discuss daily utilization — peak before and after work. The gym is structured to not support all members at one time; you need to understand capacity at peak periods. Even if there is average excess capacity, being over capacity during peak periods will cause member churn.

exhibits.title: Select figures for 1 average gym from each chain
exhibits.shows: A side-by-side table of cost and revenue line items for one average gym from each of the two chains: Gym Arnie and Gym Stallone.

framework: Profitability: Revenue (volume = # of members; price = annual membership dues, activation fees, concessions) and Costs (fixed: lease, equipment, maintenance; variable: labor, services such as towel cleaning)
Changes over time: membership growth per gym, opening new gyms
Utilization: average annual utilization and peak vs. off-peak capacity
Competitive environment: market share of each target by region and segment; market attractiveness (growth, concentration)

questions.prompt: What are the P&L line items for a single gym? After discussing, review Exhibit 1 — which gym is more attractive?
questions.guidance: Candidate should build a full P&L: revenue from membership fees and concessions, costs split into fixed (lease, maintenance, SG&A) and variable (staff/labor). After seeing Exhibit 1, candidate must recognize that while Stallone has 20% more revenue, costs are 30% higher, resulting in lower profit and margin. Intuition: Arnie is making higher margins than Stallone.

math.setup: Calculate total annual revenue per member = $600 (membership) + $5×12 (concessions) = $660. Multiply by member count for total revenue. Sum cost lines for total costs. Profit = Revenue − Costs. Margin = Profit / Revenue.
steps: Difference: Revenue +20%, Costs +30%, so cost growth outpaces revenue growth, resulting in lower profit for Stallone
math.answer: Gym Arnie: Profit $51,000, Margin 12.9%. Gym Stallone: Profit $25,200, Margin 5.3%. Gym Arnie is currently more profitable.

questions.prompt: Is there anything else we need to know? If Arnie is not growing but Stallone is growing at 10% per year, which is more attractive? How many additional members would Stallone need to match Arnie's margin?
questions.guidance: Candidate should proactively raise user/membership growth rates as a critical missing variable. Must set up a break-even equation to find the number of incremental members that would bring Stallone's margin to 12.9%. Follow-up: is 8.7% growth achievable? Candidate should flag need to confirm capacity and peak-hour constraints, marketing plan, cost of acquisition, and any incremental variable costs.

math.setup: Let x = additional members for Stallone. New profit = 25,200 + 660x. New revenue = 475,200 + 660x. Set margin equal to Arnie's 12.9%: (25,200 + 660x) / (475,200 + 660x) = 0.129.
steps: Since expected growth is 10% > 8.7% required, Stallone would exceed Arnie's margin if growth materializes
math.answer: Stallone needs approximately 63 additional members (8.7% growth) to match Arnie's 12.9% margin. At 10% projected growth, Stallone becomes more attractive.

brainstorming.prompt: What risks and qualifications should the PE firm investigate before concluding Stallone is the better acquisition?

categories.name: Capacity constraints
ideas: Peak-hour utilization may already be at or near capacity, limiting ability to add 63+ members without member churn
Need deeper due diligence on capacity at peak times (before and after work)

categories.name: Growth assumptions
ideas: 10% growth assumption may not be achievable if market has no growth
Stallone may face 'lemon' issues: lower quality equipment, poor marketing, or other structural reasons why it hasn't grown faster already

categories.name: Cost drivers
ideas: Incremental variable costs may rise with more members (additional staff, services)
Higher SG&A at Stallone could reflect structural inefficiencies rather than investment

categories.name: Member churn
ideas: Churn rate and its drivers must be understood
Acquiring new members is meaningless if existing members leave at a high rate

recommendation: Acquire Gym Stallone, assuming the economics of one gym apply to all 150 gyms and that membership can be grown by 10% without hitting capacity constraints or materially increasing variable costs
At 10% growth, Stallone's margin would exceed Arnie's current 12.9%, making it the more attractive long-term PE investment
risks: Excess capacity may be reached at peak times before 10% growth is achieved, causing member churn
Stallone may have structural issues (lower-quality equipment, poor brand, weak marketing) that explain the underperformance and would prevent growth
next_steps: Conduct deeper due diligence on peak-hour capacity at Stallone gyms
Validate the 10% growth projection through market research, historical membership trends, and benchmarking against comparable gym chains
Identify any incremental variable costs that would be triggered by higher membership
Develop a post-acquisition marketing and retention plan
